analysis.file_name: Deutsche Says The Bear Trifecta Can't All Hit At Once... But Every Relief Rally Revives The Hawks.pdf
analysis.title: Deutsche Says The Bear Trifecta Can't All Hit At Once... But Every Relief Rally Revives The Hawks
key_insights: Deutsche Bank macro strategist Henry Allen argues the three dominant bear cases (oil/Middle East escalation, AI slowdown, European fiscal stress) cannot all occur at once, because an AI scare lowers bond yields, demand-driven inflation and rate-hike odds, which eases the fiscal and inflation legs.

Most major stress points eased in recent weeks: January Brent fell from $113.43/bbl at end of October to $96.58, the Philly semiconductor index rose over 12% from its Nov 5 low through Friday, and the OAT-Bund 10-year spread fell from a 174bps peak on Oct 22 to 156bps.

The easing itself revived rate-hike pricing. The 2-year Treasury yield posted its biggest weekly jump since October 2024 (+33bps in five days), and the 10-year its biggest weekly jump since April 2025, as the S&P 500 posted its first weekly gain after four straight declines.

Three drivers undid the dovish repricing: a hot October CPI (3-month annualized core CPI of 3.75%, fastest since April 2024, which put a 50bps December hike on the table), no US-Iran deal (Trump: 'We don't need a deal with Iran'), and easier financial conditions from the tech rebound and tighter credit spreads.

Markets are pricing 113bps of Fed hikes by the September 2027 meeting (25bps already delivered plus 88bps ahead). On the day before the 2022 hiking cycle started, markets priced 95bps by the equivalent horizon, so pricing has already exceeded that starting point. Deutsche says markets consistently underestimate hiking cycles at the start.

Deutsche says investors overweight the odds of a dovish pivot whenever something breaks. With headline and core inflation both above target, it cites 2023, when the Fed and ECB kept hiking through the SVB collapse.

Oil is the one leg that does not offset the others: a crude spike raises inflation, hike odds, yields and fiscal stress while squeezing growth. The article notes Iran's Revolutionary Guards declared the Strait of Hormuz 'closed' over the weekend, the Houthis took the coast overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, a third US carrier headed to the Gulf, and a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of the strait on Monday. This weekend and Monday detail is the article author's addition, not part of Deutsche's note.
Deutsche's conclusion, as quoted: the hawkish path is favored, markets are 'once again lowballing the Fed,' and the next relief rally 'probably buys bulls nothing more than another hike.'
November realized volatility is elevated: the average daily S&P 500 move this month is 1.2%, the most since April 2025.

tension_points.bull_case: AI, oil and fiscal bear cases tend to offset: an AI scare lowers yields, demand-driven inflation and hike odds, easing the fiscal and inflation legs. Most stress points eased in recent weeks.
tension_points.bear_case: The offset also runs in reverse. A relief rally and tighter credit ease financial conditions, which revives hike pricing, as the hot CPI, no Iran deal and the equity rebound did. Oil does not offset anything and is rearming.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Hormuz-driven crude spike would break the offset logic. The hawkish path would also be validated by core CPI continuing to run at a 3.75% annualized pace.
